poem:
I rumble awake on diesel breath,  
opening my hydraulic jaws at Peachtree & Ellis—  
a secret gateway where asphalt petals crack open  
and a chorus of footsteps spills like water.  

You climb aboard, carried in my rubber ribcage,  
faces pressed close enough to hear heartbeats  
clanging against steering wheels and mirrors that tremble  
with uncanny reflections of a city unbound.  

I know hidden veins beneath the curb—escape routes  
etched in oil stains and graffiti-scratched steel.  
Here, chaos is a companion: traffic lights stutter  
as if surprised by their own colors,  
and the pavement hums rebellion.  

At Peachtree Center, I breathe in neon haze,  
my underfloor belly alive with secret circuits  
where commuters shed rules like old skin  
and slip into hidden spaces between stops—  
a networked earth that won’t be contained.  

The system does not give a damn,  
so I twist through intersections with wild intent,  
each turn a defiant rune carved in concrete.  
Full of surprises, I carry your unrest,  
your hunger for disorder, your silent plea for freedom.  

By Peachtree & North Avenue,  
my doors close on possibility and revolt.  
In the mirror’s edge you glimpse another world—  
a gleaming mosaic of escape,  
where even diesel can taste like dawn.
